p: Altan was the second son of Bars Bolud Jinong and a grandson of Dayan Khan. After Dayan Khan the Mongols formed six tümen divided into a Left Wing under the Great Khan and a Right Wing under Altan's father, who held the office of jinong, or vice-regent. Altan ruled the Tümed, whose pastures lay north of the border with Shanxi. When his elder brother Gün Bilig died in 1542, Altan became the effective leader of the Right Wing. After the death of Bodi Alagh Khan in 1547 he forced the new khagan, Darayisung Küdeng Khan, to flee eastward, and in 1551 Darayisung compromised by granting him the title Gegeen Khan.

Altan wanted to trade horses for Chinese farm produce and textiles, but the Ming court, suspicious of him, repeatedly refused and sometimes killed his envoys. He raided northern China in 1529, 1530 and 1542, and in 1550 crossed gaps in the Great Wall and besieged Beijing, setting its suburbs on fire. He strengthened his Tümed base by settling Chinese refugees there and kept a network of Ming conspirators led by Zhao Quan, a disciple of the White Lotus. In 1552 he gained control of the remains of Karakorum.

In 1570 his grandson Daičing Ejei Taiji defected to the Ming after a family quarrel. Ministers of the Longqing Emperor proposed that Altan accept a Ming title and hand over Zhao Quan in return for his grandson and trading rights. Altan agreed; Zhao and his fellow conspirators were executed, Altan was made Shunyi prince and his capital was renamed Guihua. The American Orientalist Owen Lattimore writes that the Mongols were nominally vassals, but that the Ming was eager to please them and the arrangement was more or less of benefit to both.

Altan first invited Sonam Gyatso in 1569; the lama accepted a second invitation in 1577, and Altan later had Thegchen Chonkhor, Mongolia's first monastery, built where they met. Sonam Gyatso declared Altan a reincarnation of Kublai Khan. One reason for adopting Buddhism was a fear among the Mongol elite that the peace of 1571 would spread Chinese cultural influence. Laws set out by Sonam Gyatso and instituted by Altan forbade blood sacrifices and the burning of widows. Altan died on 13 January 1582, aged 74 or 75, and his son Sengge Düüreng succeeded him as Shunyi prince. His great-grandson Yonten Gyatso was chosen as the 4th Dalai Lama in 1601.

notes: Birth: the article gives 2 January 1508 (and 'aged 74 or 75' at death); the entry's dates say 1507.
The article has the meeting accepted in 1577 and the title Dalai given in 1578; the entry's 1578 stands.
'the burning of widows' renders the article's 'immolation of women on the funeral pyres of their husbands'.
The article says Altan controlled 'the Ordos tumen' and pressed 'the Oirat Mongols in Tibet'; unclear, left out.
